LTNs are similar to schemes such as super­ blocks in Barcelona (Nieuwenhuijsen et al., 2024), and more than 100 have now been rolled out in London (Furlong et al., 2025b). Evidence as to the health impacts of LTNs includes clear evidence of a benefit in terms of reductions in road traffic injuries (Furlong et al., 2025b, 2025c); mixed evidence in terms of impacts on active travel (Aldred et al., 2024; Aldred and Goodman, 2021; Xiao et al., 2023); and evidence of a benefit in terms of reductions in noise (Leach et al., 2024). In the present study, we complement this work by extending the evidence base on how LTNs may affect health via changes in air pollution. In doing so, we also complement a wider body of literature that studies how urban trans­ portation policies affect air pollution (Khreis et al., 2023; Jafari et al., 2021), across policies ranging from car-free spaces, days and events (Glazener et al., 2022) to urban design interventions that seek to achieve mode shift towards active modes (Glazener and Khreis, 2019). A sys­ tematic review of peer-reviewed articles published between 2000 and 2020 identified 376 unique articles covering 58 unique policy in­ terventions targeted at reducing traffic-related emissions and air pollu­ tion in urban areas (Khreis et al., 2023). This review found that behavioural and land-use policies (like LTNs) were the least studied broad category of interventions. It further found that a mere 3% of included studies addressed all elements of the full-chain—traffic emis­ sions, traffic-related air pollution, exposures, and human health. Our study therefore adds to a very limited evidence base that examines the ‘full chain’ from changes in traffic through to health outcomes in rela­ tion to an intervention with behavioural and land-use elements. In common with other schemes to restrict traffic, LTNs have been controversial (Cooke et al., 2021; G¨ossling et al., 2024), and the po­ tential for increased traffic and pollution on ‘boundary roads’ has been one particular focus for this controversy (Verlinghieri et al., 2025). For example, analyses of an LTN in Birmingham found that while there were positive views about the scheme overall, there were increased tensions in the community between people living inside LTNs and those living on the boundaries (Whelan et al., 2024; Pritchett et al., 2024). Concern over the potential for increased traffic on boundary roads is also sometimes combined with claims that LTNs will disadvantage ethnic minorities, poorer residents, or residents living on roads that are already more polluted (Pritchett et al., 2024; Larrington-Spencer and Sherriff, 2025; Belcher et al., 2022). The local air pollution impacts of an LTN depend on the relative frequency of two types of change in driving behaviour. 1) Traffic evaporation: some trips stop being made by motor vehicle. This change is expected to reduce air pollution both inside the LTN and on boundary roads. Traffic evaporation is expected to decrease total pollution emissions and subsequent concentrations. 2) Traffic displacement: some trips continue to be made by motor vehicle but shift the driving route from ‘through the LTN’ to ‘on boundary roads’. This change is expected to reduce air pollution inside the LTN but increase overall emissions on boundary roads (although the increase may not be distributed evenly across bound­ ary roads). Traffic displacement is most likely to increase total emissions because the alternative routes are often more circuitous. This increase in emissions will be exacerbated if the boundary roads also become more congested, as congested ‘stop-start’ traffic emits more pollution. From a theoretical perspective, it is therefore not clear whether LTNs will typically increase or decrease pollution on boundary roads, nor whether they typically increase or decrease total pollution. Empirical evidence on these points is therefore required. The existing empirical evidence base is, however, currently limited to a few studies. We are aware of only a single peer-reviewed study that empirically measures the air quality impacts of LTN schemes using a controlled, longitudinal design. This study used direct measurements of air quality and found that, relative to control areas, average pollution concentrations fell inside three London LTNs and in their surrounding areas (Yang et al., 2022). Besides this, several London local authorities have commissioned studies that model the air quality impacts of indi­ vidual LTNs, based on measured before-and-after changes in traffic volumes. These latter studies typically report beneficial effects inside LTNs and a mixture of beneficial, negligible and adverse effects across different boundary roads (CERC, 2021; CERC, 2022; AECOM, 2022). Outside of London, one local authority monitoring report finds pollution decreases inside three LTNs in Oxford and a mixture of beneficial, negligible and adverse effects on boundary roads (Oxford City Council, 2023); and one evaluation from Barcelona reports decreases in NO2 and/or black carbon inside two new superblocks, alongside no overall changes in these pollutants in the immediately surrounding area (P´erez et al., 2025). In addition to these empirical evaluations, some interna­ tional papers have modelled the potential impacts of superblock schemes based on estimates of how traffic volumes or tree cover might change (Mueller et al., 2020; Rodriguez-Rey et al., 2022; Li and Wilson, 2023). The existing evidence base thus comprises relatively few studies, many of which cover just a single LTN scheme. In addition, existing modelling studies only model pollution impacts as a function of changes in traffic volumes, without additionally considering changes in conges­ tion. A further limitation of existing studies is that they do not consider the distribution of impacts in relation to characteristics such as ethnicity, socio-economic status and baseline air pollution levels. The present study addresses these research gaps by modelling the air pollution impacts of five LTNs spread across Greater London, using high- resolution pre- and post-traffic and speed/congestion data as inputs. We then model the spatial distribution of these impacts and how these changes in air pollution affect mortality, years of life lost, and childhood asthma incidence. 2. Methods 2.1. LTNs included in the study Drawing on extensive empirical data, we carried out air quality modelling to estimate the health impact of air pollution changes due to the introduction of five LTNs in London. The five schemes we studied are described in Table 1 and shown in Fig. 1. We modelled air pollution impacts both inside the LTNs and across their surrounding areas. We defined the modelled area covered in terms of Output Areas (OAs), which are administrative census areas covering around 330 people each. Specifically, we modelled impacts across all OAs that were within 200m of any road that experienced a traffic vol­ ume change in our scenarios, or that were within a 1-km2 grid in which minor road emissions changed. These OAs covered all areas within 250m of the five LTNs and extended up to a maximum of 2 km from LTNs. 2.2. Overview of modelling approach We implemented a full-chain model (Khreis et al., 2018) outlined in Fig. 2 and described briefly below, with full details in Supplementary Material 1. This model 1) used extensive empirical data to estimate traffic volumes, speeds and vehicle types as of 2023, in and around the five LTNs (red boxes in Fig. 2); 2) converted these into estimated traffic-related air pollutant emissions (orange boxes); 3) combined these emissions with other data sources to model air pollutant dispersion and concentrations (green boxes); and 4) converted air pollution concen­ trations into select attributable health impacts (blue boxes). We imple­ mented scenarios with and without LTNs, in which we varied the first element of this model (traffic volumes, speeds and vehicle types) while leaving all other elements unchanged and compared the impacts of the LTNs on pollutant concentrations and the select health outcomes. Our implementation of step 1) involved bespoke data manipulation and the novel use of traffic speed data. Our implementation of steps 2), 3) and 4) largely drew on standard ap­ proaches derived from peer-reviewed literature, albeit with custom­ isation to the London setting. Before implementing the model shown in Fig. 2, we conducted a validation exercise in which we set up a similar model that utilised traffic and air pollution emission data to model air pollution concen­ trations in 2019 (i.e. equivalent to the first three stages of the full-chain model: details in Supplementary Material 1). We compared the resulting modelled air pollution concentrations to pollution measurements taken in 2019 from two available continuous monitors (measuring PM10 and NO2) and 83 diffusion tubes (measuring NO2) within 1 km of the LTNs. Across the five LTNs, 50% of modelled concentrations were within 10% of measured values for PM10 (N = 1/2) and 51% for NO2 (N = 43/85). 100% of modelled concentrations were within 25% for PM10 (N = 2/2) and 93% for NO2 (N = 79/85, with five of the remaining six sites located ≥500m away from the LTNs and their boundary roads). In addition, metrics for bias, correlation and error indicated good statistical perfor­ mance, and the average modelled pollution concentrations were within 6% of the average measured concentrations for both pollutants. In line with DEFRA guidance (DEFRA, 2025), we considered these results to indicate acceptable accuracy in our model and an adequate baseline set-up. 2.3. Background traffic volumes The London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (LAEI) estimates traffic flows and speeds by vehicle type for all major roads in London, and models minor road traffic on a 1 km2 background grid (Gla and Tfl Air Quality, 2021). We took the 2019 LAEI data as our starting point, as this is the latest year that pre-dated both the Covid-19 pandemic and the implementation of our five LTNs. The LAEI provided traffic volumes for seven vehicle types: motorbikes, cars, taxis, light goods vehicles, buses/coaches, rigid heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) and articulated HGVs. We then used Department for Transport traffic count data (Department for Transport, 2024) from 2019 to 2023 to a) cross-check the 2019 total traffic volumes on major roads near our LTNs, and b) to project the 2019 traffic volumes forward to 2023. We used these LAEI data to capture traffic volumes and speeds on all roads for which sce­ nario traffic data were not collected. 2.3.2. Scenario traffic data To model how traffic volumes changed in scenarios with and without LTNs, we used before-and-after monitoring data published by the four local authorities that implemented our five LTNs (see Table 1 for numbers of count points and dates of data collection). For internal roads that lacked traffic count data and that were captured by LAEI in the 1 km2 minor roads grid (rather than being modelled explicitly), we adjusted the entire 1 km2 grid by that LTN's internal-road traffic volume change factor, as scaled by the proportion of the area of that 1 km2 grid covered by the LTN. Note that this approach accurately captures area-wide changes in traffic but misallocates some of that change to areas outside the LTN rather than inside the LTN. Finally, we assumed there was no change in traffic volumes on roads that had no monitoring data and that were neither internal to the LTN nor boundary roads. This is expected to be a conservative assumption if there is traffic evaporation. Changes in traffic flows were assumed to apply pro rata to all seven vehicle types except buses and coaches. Bus and coach traffic flows were assumed to remain unchanged between the ‘without an LTN’ and ‘with an LTN’ scenarios because none of our five LTNs involved a change in bus routes or bus frequency. 2.3.3. Scenario speed data Previous efforts to model the air pollution impacts of LTNs have only varied traffic volumes (AECOM, 2022; CERC, 2021; CERC, 2022), and assumed no change in traffic speeds and congestion. However, previous research has found evidence that average traffic speeds fall, and congestion increases, on boundary roads in the first year post-LTN implementation (Furlong et al., in preparation).1 This matters because motor vehicles emit more air pollution at slower average speeds with regular start-stop driving, with the Emissions Factors Toolkit v12.0 indicating that this particularly applies at speeds below around 8 km/h (DEFRA, 2023). We therefore modelled speed, and congestion impacts on boundary roads as follows. First, the LTN boundary roads were divided into seg­ ments around 200m to 500m in length. The same was done for boundary road segments around matched control areas (see Table 1 for numbers of segments). Modelled scenarios Table 2 captures the five scenarios we modelled, using different traffic and speed data measured at different time points. The Baseline scenario captures our estimate of pollution concentrations in the absence of the LTN schemes, and we compared all other scenarios to this. The remaining four scenarios capture estimates of pollution con­ centrations in the presence of LTNs, with the Latest Data scenario being our primary scenario of interest. This Latest Data scenario uses the most recent data available for each LTN, which corresponds to the Year 1 scenario for Streatham Wells, the Year 2a scenario for Stoke Newington, Camden Square and Brixton Hill, and the Year 2b scenario for St Ann's. In running our scenarios, each LTN was considered independently. This meant that, for example, the estimated impacts of the Streatham Wells LTN were not affected by the implementation of Brixton Hill LTN nearby. 2.4. Part 2: modelling traffic emissions The Emissions Factors Toolkit (Version 12.0, December 2023) was used to estimate the NOx, primary NO2, PM10 and PM2.5 emissions resulting from a given set of inputs on traffic volumes and traffic speeds. This process involved applying average speed-dependent emission fac­ tors, as taken from the COPERT emission calculator Version 5.6 (September 2022; https://copert.emisia.com/). Different emission fac­ tors were used for each of the seven vehicle types modelled, with further subdivisions according to Emissions Factors Toolkit fleet projections for fuel type (petrol versus diesel), Euro emission standard category and engine size. To account for discrepancies between the COPERT emission factors and real-world emissions, we adjusted the COPERT emission factors based on published remote sensing data (Mehlig et al., 2023). We initially estimated traffic emissions at the hourly level by applying a time-varying emissions profile to the estimated daily average traffic flows. For LTN boundary roads, the time-varying emissions pro­ file was estimated using road-specific hourly speed and congestion Google API data (see previous section). For all other roads, we applied a default time-varying profile of traffic emissions, as derived using data from London by Beevers et al. (2009). The estimated hourly emissions were then used to create diurnal profiles and average daily emission rates for each modelled road. 2.5. Part 3: modelling air pollution concentrations We used the Atmospheric Dispersion Modelling System (ADMS)- Urban model (Version 5.0.1.3; http://www.cerc.co.uk/environmental-s oftware/ADMS-Urban-model.html). This model is widely used for air quality management and policy assessment by local, metropolitan and national governments in the UK and worldwide. Model inter- comparison evaluations have shown that the model performs well in predicting pollution concentrations (Heist et al., 2013; Carslaw et al., 2013). As illustrated in Fig. 2, ADMS-Urban takes as inputs traffic emissions data alongside non-road emissions, land use characteristics, meteorological data, and background concentrations. It uses these as the basis for modelling of how air pollution is generated and dispersed in ambient air and spatially. It produces output in the form of hourly air pollution concentrations with high spatial resolution determined by the user. The following were our key inputs. Non-road emissions: All large industrial sources within 10 km of the LTNs were modelled explicitly as point sources. Emissions for all other non-road sources, including industrial sources more than 10 km from the LTNs, were estimated for 2023 by interpolating between the 2019 and the 2025 values in LAEI. The LAEI includes spatially distributed emis­ sions for 26 non-road groups, including commercial and domestic emissions, industrial emissions, rail, shipping, and construction. These other non-road emissions were modelled as aggregated 1 km2 resolution grid sources covering the whole of London. We derived hourly and monthly profiles for these grid source emissions from European Moni­ toring and Evaluation Programme (EMEP) emissions data (Denier van der Gon et al., 2011). Parameters used in ADMS-Urban to represent the effect of land use on dispersion • Surface roughness length: This affects wind speed and turbulence, which in turn affects air pollution dispersion. We used a value of 1m; a typical value for a built-up area. • Monin-Obukhov length: This captures the stability of the atmo­ sphere. In cities, urban heat island effects mean that the Monin- Obukhov length will never fall below some minimum value in sta­ ble conditions. In line with previous work in London (CERC, 2024), our model used a minimum value of 75m. • Urban canopy flow: The flow field that drives dispersion of pollutants within an urban area is not homogeneous: buildings displace the upwind wind speed profile above the building canopy and reduce in- canopy wind speeds. The ADMS-Urban spatially varying urban can­ opy flow option captures this on a neighbourhood-by- neighbourhood basis. In our model we used derived inputs for Lon­ don (Jackson et al., 2016). • Street canyons: The presence of buildings can create street canyon effects that result in pollutants being trapped. We captured this using the ADMS Advanced Canyon option, taking building footprint data from OpenStreetMap and elevation data from the Environment Agency National LIDAR programme. Meteorological data: We used hourly sequential meteorological data measured at Heathrow Airport across 2023. Background data: The modelling used the ADMS-Urban NOx photolytic chemistry module, which uses the Generic Reaction Set of equations to account for fast, near-road oxidation of NO by O3 to form NO2, and which uses simple sulphate chemistry to account for the conversion of SO2 to PM2.5 and PM10. The chemistry schemes are calculated on an hourly basis and require background pollution con­ centrations, in addition to source emissions. We explicitly modelled direct emissions of NOx, NO2, PM10 and PM2.5 from all sources in Greater London. We also estimated the back­ ground concentrations of NOx, NO2, ozone, PM10 and PM2.5 in air car­ ried into London from outside the area. These estimates of background concentrations came from air pollution monitors in four rural locations outside of London, with hourly data taken from whichever site best matched the wind direction for that hour. In order to discount hours affected by local sources of particulate matter at these rural sites, these data were supplemented with measurements of PM10 and PM2.5 from London suburban and background sites (see Supplementary Material 1). Output points, contour maps and OA-level averages: Within each LTN's output domain, concentrations were calculated on a regular grid of output points with a resolution of 20m, with additional sets of points added along the major roads where the concentration gradient is steepest (see Supplementary Material 1 for details). We used this model output to generate 2m resolution contour maps using the natural neighbour interpolation method. Average pollution concentrations were calculated at the OA level for each scenario as a simple average of all 2m by 2m concentration cells in each OA. 2.6. Part 4: modelling health impacts Impacts on mortality and years of life lost (YLLs) were modelled via a joint function of both NO2 and PM2.5, using concentration response functions of 1.024 for a 10 μg/m3 increase in NO2 adjusted for PM2.5; and 1.035 for a 5 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 adjusted for NO2 (Chen et al., 2024). These estimates come from a meta-analysis of population-level studies looking at the effect of average pollution concentrations at participants’ homes, as modelled largely at the residential address level or at the small-area level and without accounting for individual mobility and variations beyond the residential location. They are therefore considered appropriate to apply to the OA-level average pollution con­ centrations that we estimated (OAs being the smallest Census geography level), and this is standard practice when conducting health impact as­ sessments of air pollution. The number of deaths attributable to air pollution was calculated by sex and 5-year age band for each OA. In line with recommendations from Public Health England guidance for estimating local mortality burdens (Gowers et al., 2014), mortality attributable to long-term exposure to air pollution was based on the number of deaths in adults aged 30 years or more. This calculation involved combining a) the attributable fraction of deaths in each OA, as derived based on the relevant concentration response functions plus the average pollutant concentration for that OA in a given scenario; b) the number of people aged 30 years or over living in that OA in 2023, by sex and age band, and c) borough level age-standardised all-cause mortality rates in 2023 (available from https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/) To calculate the number of YLLs per OA due to air pollution, we multiplied the 5-year age band and sex-specific attributable deaths by the corresponding borough-level 2021-2023 period life expectancy for each group (ONS, 2024). Impacts on childhood asthma incidence were modelled twice, first as a function of NO2 (1.05 per 4 μg/m3 increase in NO2), and second as a function of PM2.5 (1.03 per 1 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5), using single- pollutant concentration response functions from the meta-analysis by Khreis et al. (2017). Results modelled via both NO2 and PM2.5 are pre­ sented in text, to give a range of plausible results and are not meant to be summed. The number of new cases of childhood asthma per year was calculated by combining a) the attributable fraction of asthma in each OA, based on the average pollutant concentration for that OA in a given scenario; b) the number of children aged 0 to 18 living in that OA in 2023, and c) the Global Burden of Disease estimated asthma incidence in Greater London in 2023 (available from https://vizhub.healthdata. org/gbd-results/). 2.7. Statistical analysis We first examined average effects across the different scenarios modelled (Table 2), to assess whether air pollution impacts changed according to which year of ‘after’ data was used. We then proceeded to focus on comparing the Latest Data scenario to the Baseline scenario for more detailed analysis. Our primary outcomes were the absolute changes in PM2.5 and NO2 concentrations, plus their resulting impacts on mortality and asthma. To provide context for these absolute changes, we also present the results in terms of relative changes and, in the case of air pollution concentrations, relative to background improvements in air pollution. Specifically, UK government estimates of background air pollution concentrations (DEFRA, 2024) indicate that all-source background NO2 fell by an average of 0.85 μg/m3 between 2023 and 2024 in the relevant areas of London, while PM2.5 fell by 0.07 μg/m3. This allowed us to quantify the modelled LTN-related changes in terms of ‘number of days of pro­ gress/delay’ relative to this favourable background trend – i.e. how far had the LTN accelerated, or delayed, air quality improvements in Lon­ don relative to the observed background trend. For instance, one would describe the LTN as ‘accelerating progress by 365 days’ if the LTN were estimated to reduce NO2 pollution by 0.85 μg/m3, as that is equal to the background annual improvement in NO2. We conducted our analyses of pollution impacts at the OA level. To capture average effects, we took simple means across OAs. To calculate confidence intervals we used the ‘acreg’ package in Stata (Colella et al., 2023), fitting the ‘spatial’ command to take account of spatial clustering between OAs; specifying 2 km as the maximum distance between which the error terms of OAs were assumed to be correlated; and using the ‘bartlett’ option to impose a distance linear decay between the error terms of nearby OAs. The 2 km threshold was chosen as it comfortably spans LTNs and boundary roads, and also as trialling various thresholds indicated that 2 km resulted in conservative (least significant) estimates. These confidence intervals capture uncertainty only due to variation H. Khreis et al. Environmental Research 306 (2026) 125093 7 between OAs and allowed us to assess how far any differences between different groups of OAs (e.g. different LTNs) might be due to chance. In our primary analyses, we looked at average effects across the 929 OAs in the five LTNs modelled, treating these as a single sample. This approach captures average air pollution impacts in these five schemes. In sensitivity analyses, we instead ran a two-stage process that first calculated average effects for each of the LTNs separately and then used random-effects meta-analysis to pool the results across the five LTNs. This approach captures the estimated air pollution impacts for a ‘typical’ LTN in London and produced similar findings. A further set of sensitivity analyses excluded Camden Square, because Camden Square is the smallest LTN in our study, and is the only LTN that a) used ‘before’ data collected before Covid-19, and b) saw boundary roads traffic decrease in the ‘with LTNs’ scenario. As previously mentioned, the potential for increased pollution on boundary roads is typically a leading point of controversy in relation to LTNs, and this is sometimes combined with claims that this will disad­ vantage ethnic minorities, poorer residents, or residents living on roads that are already more polluted. We therefore sought to examine the spatial distribution of the impacts of our five LTNs, as well as examining variation between the five schemes. We did so by defining the following five small-area characteristics at the OA level. 1) LTN scheme: i.e. Stoke Newington Church Street, Camden Square, St Ann's, Brixton Hill, or Streatham Wells 2) OA area type, defined as: • Inside the LTN: defined as >50% of the OA's buildings lie inside the LTN, plus <20m of the boundary roads intersect the OA. • On the LTN boundary roads: defined as ≥20m of the boundary roads intersect the OA, and/or the boundary road runs directly alongside the OA. • Other external areas: OAs that did not meet the two above definitions. 3) Proportion of non-White residents in the 2021 Census. 4) Mean number of deprivation dimensions per household in the 2021 Census (covering domains of employment; education; health and disability; and household overcrowding). 5) Average NO2 concentrations in our baseline model. The final three of these small-area characteristics were divided into quarters on an LTN-by-LTN basis (i.e. ‘most deprived quarter from Stoke Newington’ through to ‘least deprived quarter from Stoke Newington’, and likewise for the other LTNs). This was done in order to adjust for scheme effects (i.e. Stoke Newington versus Camden Square etc.) when examining the distribution of impacts. To test for heterogeneity across these groups, we ran successive single-variable linear regression models (using the ‘acreg’ package, as described above) that entered the relevant OA-characteristic as a categorical variable. We then performed a Wald test for heterogeneity. This was done for each variable in turn in separate models, without adjusting for co-variates, because our primary concern was the raw spatial distribution of the attributable health impacts (e.g. ‘do average effects differ between poorer and richer areas?’), rather than the identification of independently causal predictors (e.g. ‘do average effects differ between poorer and richer areas, after adjusting for base­ line pollution levels?’). When examining health impacts, we summed OA-level estimates to generate aggregated estimates of total impact. 3. Results 3.1. Baseline pollution levels and mapping results In the ‘without LTNs’ Baseline scenarios, average pollution concen­ trations across the areas we modelled were 18.9 μg/m3 for NO2 and 8.4 μg/m3 for PM2.5. These values are below the current legal limits in the UK (40 μg/m3 for NO2 and 25 μg/m3 for PM2.5), but above the air quality guideline values proposed by the World Health Organisation (10 μg/m3 for NO2 and 5 μg/m3 for PM2.5). Our results indicated a reduction in pollution on most streets inside LTNs, whereas on boundary roads there was a mix of pollution increases and decreases. This is illustrated in the map shown in Fig. 3, with Supplementary Material 2 showing maps for all schemes and pollutants. 3.2. Comparison of scenarios: how air pollution impacts change as schemes become longer established Table 3 presents average changes in air pollution in the three sce­ narios, across the areas inside and surrounding the five LTNs. As Table 3 shows, average concentrations fell for both NO2 and PM2.5 in the first year of scheme implementation (Year 1 scenario). In the four LTNs with available data, a reduction in congestion between Year 1 and Year 2 led to a further modest fall in average NO2 concentrations but had little effect on PM2.5 (Year 2a scenario). In the one LTN with available data, the reduction in congestion and traffic between Year 1 and Year 2 led to a more substantial further decrease in both NO2 and PM2.5 (Year 2b scenario). These results were similar in analyses restricted to peak-time air pollution concentrations (see Supplementary Material 3), and in analyses that sought to estimate impacts in a ‘typical’ LTN (see Supplementary Material 3). In the remainder of the results section, we use the Latest Data sce­ nario for each of the five LTNs as a proxy for long-term air pollution impacts. 3.3. Average air pollution effects using latest available scenario data Using the latest available scenario data for each LTN, the average change across the five LTNs and their surrounding areas was −0.034 μg/ m3 in NO2 (95%CI -0.056 to −0.011) and −0.0051 μg/m3 in PM2.5 (95% CI -0.0077 to −0.0025: see also Table 4). Similarly, in analyses that used random-effects meta-analysis to estimate impacts in a ‘typical’ LTN, the change was −0.044 μg/m3 in NO2 (95%CI -0.082 to −0.006) and −0.0062 μg/m3 in PM2.5 (95%CI -0.0103 to −0.0021). As context, these observed average changes across the five LTNs correspond to a mean −0.18% relative decrease in NO2 as compared to the estimated level of 18.9 μg/m3 in the ‘without LTNs’ scenario; and −0.06% mean relative decrease in PM2.5 as compared to the estimated level of 8.4 μg/m3 in the ‘without LTNs’ scenario. Relative to back­ ground improvements in air pollution in London between 2023 and 2024, this is equivalent to gaining an average of 14 days of progress in relation to NO2 and gaining 27 days of progress in relation to PM2.5. In other words, across the five LTNs and their surrounding areas, the beneficial average effects were statistically significant but were small. 3.4. Distribution of air pollution effects according to selected area characteristics When looking at LTNs individually, all five schemes were modelled as having a decrease in average NO2 and PM2.5 concentrations in the latest data (see Supplementary Material 3 for LTN-level results for all three scenarios, and Supplementary Material 2 for contour maps). Health impacts of air pollution changes Table 5 shows the estimated changes in deaths, YLLs and incident cases of childhood asthma attributable to the implementation of the five LTNs and the associated modelled reductions in air pollution. Across the 307,734 people living in and around the five LTNs, we estimated that on average there were 1481 deaths and 22,023 YLLs per year in the ‘without LTNs’ Baseline scenario. Discussion 4.1. Summary This study uses extensive empirical data alongside a full-chain modelling approach to model the impacts of five low traffic neigh­ bourhoods (LTNs) in London on NO2 and PM2.5 concentrations, plus select associated health outcomes. The model inputs included observed before-and-after traffic count, traffic speed and congestion data. We found that LTNs led to statistically significant but small decreases in NO2 and PM2.5 concentrations. This decrease reflected a combination of 1) a mixture of pollution increases and decreases in surrounding boundary areas, which largely cancelled each other out; plus 2) consistent (but modest) pollution decreases inside the LTNs. There was no statistically significant evidence that the average improvement in air quality varied by ethnic diversity or deprivation, but there was evidence that areas with the highest baseline pollution saw the smallest benefits. The overall improvements in average air quality translated into benefits in terms of mortality and childhood asthma, but the effects were very small (0.01% to 0.04% area-wide, 0.05% to 0.19% inside the LTNs). We conclude that LTNs typically improve air quality and public health in London but, at the current modest scale of implementation, their effect is small. 4.2. The validated baseline configu­ ration demonstrated good performance and was consistent with estab­ lished regulatory and scientific guidance. Our analysis advances previous work in several important ways: by examining multiple LTNs across London; by integrating speed and congestion metrics alongside traffic volume data; and by assessing the distribution of impacts at a fine spatial (small-area) scale. In addition to mortality, which is commonly included in similar assessments, we estimated health impacts related to childhood morbidity, an outcome that remains comparatively under­ studied. Collectively, these contributions add to the limited empirical evidence on the effectiveness of LTNs and provide new insights into their implications for environmental justice and health equity. Our study also has some important limitations, most of which are expected to be conservative – i.e. to have led us to underestimate the beneficial effects of LTNs. First, we were limited in the traffic data available to us, creating structural uncertainty in our estimates that is not captured in our confidence intervals. In particular, most of the measurement points were inside the LTNs or on immediately sur­ rounding boundary roads, meaning we had to assume no change in traffic on more distant roads. Another structural uncertainty was our use of rather coarse 1 km2 grids to assign minor road emissions, which may tend to underestimate benefits inside the LTNs. These uncertainties could usefully be assessed in future sensitivity analyses, and compared to other sources of uncertainty in the full modelling chain such as the input data parameters themselves and the assumptions and processes underpinning the emission, dispersion and health simulation models. Second, we were limited to using ‘after’ data collected one or at most two years after the schemes were implemented. Our findings suggest that the air pollution impacts of LTNs become more favourable over time, which is consistent with the general expectation that it may take some time to realise the full mode shift benefits of road reallocation schemes (Cairns et al., 2002; Furlong et al., in preparation). It is there­ fore an important limitation that we did not have access to longer follow-up data, and our findings may underestimate the longer-term air quality benefits of LTNs. Future studies should measure or model this when longer-term data becomes available, and include other more specific traffic-related pollutants, as discussed next. Third, we only modelled air pollution effects via NO2 and PM2.5. Although these are traditionally the two key pollutants used to model air quality impacts on health, we note that recent studies highlight the growing significance of black carbon due to its strong associations with adverse health outcomes (Redaelli et al., 2019). Black carbon, a component of particulate matter, is also a particularly sensitive indicator of traffic-related emissions and may show more pronounced reductions following traffic restriction interventions compared to broader particu­ late matter measures. Black carbon is therefore a worthwhile pollutant for future studies on LTNs and other urban transport policies to model explicitly or measure directly. In addition, our study also does not model ozone (O3) directly. O3 is often negatively associated with NO2 in urban areas and reductions in NOx emissions can, in some contexts, trigger increases in O3. O3 may therefore have increased slightly with the implementation of the LTNs. This is not expected to have materially affected our estimates of health impacts, however, as we used NO2 concentration response functions that were estimated without adjust­ ment for O3. As such, these estimates may be interpreted as reflecting the effects of NO2 within the broader pollutant mixture which includes O3. Future work could benefit from explicitly modelling O3 alongside other pollutants and including concentration response functions which appropriately account for O3 and potential interactive effects. Fourth, we only modelled health impacts in terms of mortality/years of life lost and childhood asthma. Total health impacts would have been larger had we included the many health outcomes that have been associated with traffic-related air pollution (Health Effects Institute, 2022). Fifth, in the present study we only model air pollution effects at the local level. Yet air pollution disperses, and most traffic-related back­ ground air pollution in London is not generated locally. Specifically, DEFRA produce 1 km2 resolution background concentration maps which provide source apportionment of NOx concentrations by source group (traffic, industry, domestic etc.) and source location (inside versus outside each 1 km2 grid square). In Greater London in 2023, these DEFRA maps estimate that on average around four times more back­ ground NOx pollution came from traffic outside a given grid square than from traffic inside that grid square (23% from traffic outside, 5% from traffic inside, and 72% from other sources) (DEFRA, 2024). This means that if one achieved London-wide the same relative reduction in traffic that we observed in and around our LTNs, the London-wide relative decrease in NO2 would likely be several times larger than was estimated in this study. Future simulation studies would be useful to investigate this point. Finally, we recognise that air pollution is only one of the pathways whereby LTNs may affect population health, and that a holistic assess­ ment of health impacts will be more informative for policymakers (Glazener et al., 2021). Our wider study has previously reported that London's LTNs reduce traffic injuries inside LTNs by a third (and decrease injuries on boundary roads for some groups or locations) (Furlong et al., 2025b, 2025c). We are currently working on estimating the physical activity impacts of the schemes, and on comparing the magnitude of impacts across those different pathways. 4.3. Most of the existing evi­ dence base consists of studies that, like the present study, model air quality impacts based on changes in traffic counts. These previous modelling studies align with the present study in finding larger air quality benefits for NO2 than PM2.5, which is expected since NO2 is the more specific marker of traffic-related air pollution. These previous modelling studies also generally align with the present study in finding that 1) the air quality benefits inside LTNs are relatively small; and 2) that surrounding boundary roads experience a mixture of positive and negative effects, which to some extent cancel each other out. For instance, in the present study we found average NO2 changes of −0.87% inside the LTN areas, and −0.18% in boundary road areas (or +0.03% in a sensitivity analysis which removed Camden Square LTN). By contrast, the only previous controlled study that measured air pollution directly (using NO2 monitors around three LTNs in a single borough) found much larger effects, with NO2 changes of −5.7% inside the LTN areas and −8.9% in boundary and surrounding areas (Yang et al., 2022). This discrepancy is puzzling, particularly the large air quality benefit for boundary and surrounding areas. We therefore think it would be valuable to conduct further controlled before-and-after studies that directly measure air pollution in and around new LTNs. In interpreting our findings, we think it important to consider two further points from the wider literature on this topic. The first point is that interventions may achieve proportionally greater impacts when scaled up to the city level as compared to when implemented in just a few local areas. For instance, when Mueller et al. (2020) considered the potential effects of scaling Barcelona's superblocks across the whole city, they estimated that the pollution benefits could be substantial (e.g. −24.3% in NO2 pollution, city-wide), driven by large modelled modal shifts. At present, London is very far from having LTNs implemented city wide: as of June 2024, an estimated 5% of Londoners live in an LTN (Furlong et al., 2025b), and implementation is generally slow and piecemeal. If LTNs were implemented city-wide, we would expect larger proportional air quality benefits for two reasons. First, as discussed above, our model is limited to a focus on local air quality benefits. Because air pollution disperses, our model is expected to underestimate several-fold the relative air quality benefits of city-wide LTNs. In other words, a 10% reduction in local traffic delivers substantially smaller local air quality benefits than a 10% reduction in city-wide traffic. Second, more speculatively, it seems possible to us that the traffic reduction impacts of LTNs might scale in a non-linear way, with greater effects per LTN above a certain threshold of implementation. For instance, the approximately 10% reduction in local traffic that we observed after implementing a single LTN might become, say, a 20% reduction in city-wide traffic if implementing LTNs city-wide. The second point is that cities are expected to achieve the biggest air quality benefits when they combine road-reallocation policies like LTNs with other measures such as clean air zones. For instance, in a scenario modelling study from Barcelona, Rodriguez-Rey et al. (2022) found that the largest NO2 reductions were estimated when superblocks (which are similar to LTNs) were implemented alongside a clean air zone. This is in line with best practice when it comes to generating policy options, where packaging sustainable urban mobility policies is recommended as the gold standard as it can increase acceptability, effectiveness, and impact (Khreis et al., 2023, May et al., 2018). In London, a clean air zone (the “Ultra Low Emission Zone”) was progressively rolled out across the city between 2019 and 2023, contributing to substantial improvements to air quality, particularly on busy main roads (GLA and TFL, 2025). We consider such policies highly complementary to LTNs, as they mitigate the modest negative air pollution impacts that LTNs have on some boundary roads. In other words, if LTNs are implemented alongside a strong clean air zone or similar interventions, even boundary roads that experience an increase in traffic may experience a decrease in pollution. 4.4. Environmental justice implications One of the central debates around urban traffic interventions is their impact on environmental justice, that is, whether they improve or worsen already entrenched exposure disparities. When we stratified areas by proportion of non-White residents and by levels of household deprivation, we found pollution decreases in all areas, with no statisti­ cally significant differences across these groups in the magnitude of this improvement. Our ability to detect inequitable effects was, however, constrained by modest sample sizes, small effect sizes and the fact we only analysed five LTNs. This makes it possible that inequitable impacts existed that we were not statistically powered to detect. Further inves­ tigation of the spatial impacts of LTNs would therefore be valuable, across a larger number of LTNs. In addition, we did find evidence that areas with the highest baseline NO2 levels benefited the least. We note that the areas in our study with the highest baseline pollution typically lay alongside main roads, which do not generally receive any traffic restrictions when an LTN is imple­ mented but instead become boundary roads. This finding of smaller benefits on roads with higher baseline pollution is therefore in line with our finding of smaller benefits in boundary areas than inside the LTNs. In interpreting these findings, it is important to note that we did not find evidence that on average there was a harm either to the most polluted quarter of areas (change −0.01% in NO2) or to boundary road areas in general (change −0.18% in NO2). This finding is in line with previous evidence that there is no large, systematic increase in traffic on boundary roads (Thomas and Aldred, 2024). Our study therefore in­ dicates the inaccuracy of a common theme of opposition to LTNs, namely “LTNs […] have proven time and time again to increase con­ gestion/pollution” (G¨ossling et al., 2024). Nevertheless, the fact that the benefits were small to negligible on the most polluted roads does demonstrate the potential for LTNs to exacerbate pre-existing inequalities in air pollution exposure and this is a key area for policy intervention. Moreover, although we found no net harm to boundary roads on average, we did find increases in traffic and pollution on some specific roads. We believe these findings further reinforce the case for implementing LTNs as part of a package of transport policies, with measures like LTNs (which bring the largest benefits to minor roads) coupled with other measures like clean air zones, fuel taxes or price increases, alternative fuel and vehicle tech­ nologies, or diesel surcharges (which bring the largest benefits to main roads). We also consider that local authorities should monitor all LTN boundary roads carefully to identify those specific road segments which experience traffic increases and should adaptively target those boundary roads that are negatively affected with additional local mitigation measures. A synthesis of 58 unique urban policy interventions to reduce traffic-related air pollution in cities can be found in Khreis et al. (2023). 5. Conclusions We conclude that LTNs do typically improve air quality at the local level, which translates into benefits in terms of mortality and childhood asthma incidence. Their average effect is small, however, and largely confined to the areas inside the schemes. Impacts appear broadly equi­ table by small-area ethnic diversity and deprivation, however areas with higher baseline pollution (which typically lie alongside main roads) benefit the least and warrant further targeted intervention. LTNs should therefore be seen as complementing, not replacing, broader policies like clean air zones, clean bus fleets, and road user charging. We find that, despite being a prominent concern in the opposition to LTNs (Verlinghieri et al., 2025), boundary road areas do not experience an increase in modelled air pollution on average. We do, however, find that pollution increases by a small to moderate amount on some specific boundary roads (as offset by decreases on other boundary roads). This highlights a need for granular monitoring of traffic and air pollution impacts, which can be used for iterative scheme refinement to address or H. Khreis et al. As cities around the world implement and expand traffic reduction measures, policy makers should situate LTNs within broader, justice- oriented urban environmental strategies, and commit to ongoing, evidence-based monitoring and adjustment. Advisory group meeting 1 24 July 2024 1pm – 5pm Advisory group member attendees: Gary Fuller (Chair) – Imperial College London, UK (GF) Elizabeth Fu – AirParif, France (EF) David Carslaw – University of York, UK (DC) Ludo Vandenthoren – Mutualités Libres, Belgium (LV) Martin Lutz – Formerly head of air quality management at Berlin City Government, Berlin (ML) Anna Font – IMT Nord Europe, France (AF) Transport for London (TfL) Greater London Authority (GLA) Actions: DC: Provide briefing note with further information on Defra/national data available DC: Provide information/ reports on an alternative for LOESS smoothing AF: Send over advice on statistical techniques DC: Information/reports on advanced “leave-out cross-validation” methods LV: Link to report/ slides for the health impacts study in Belgium EF: Provide Paris LEZ assessment methodology links GLA: Send the published London-wide ULEZ Six Month Report ALL: Send any relevant reports/research links Notes: Introductions • Introductions from all members, including brief summary of their experience of air pollution and low emission zone assessments. Terms of Reference • Discussion about purpose of the advisory group. • Opportunity for questions on the terms of reference. • Confirmation that all members of the group agree with the terms of reference. Overview • Overview of GLA and TfL people and processes. • Overview of ULEZ policy – what it is, phased expansions, reporting schedules. • Overview of past methodology (Inner London) and current methodology (Outer London expansion). Method Discussion – selection of ULEZ border area • Consider that current method may be understating the impact of the scheme. • Discussed reasoning for 40 km zone as a control / counterfactual to the ULEZ intervention area (avoiding coastal areas/thinking about weather etc, no Clean Air Zones (CAZ) in this area). Method Discussion – nation-wide data for other cities • Group wondered if ANPR data is available from other cities. • ULEZ cameras give more accurate picture for London than the data from Defra/estimated fleets. Method Discussion –fleet composition • Historical fleet data is available over multiple years from the ULEZ monitoring system. Method uses evidence from central and inner London and includes natural churn when estimating the “No-ULEZ scenario” for emissions. • Discussion of cross-border effect of fleet turnover due to the ULEZ (i.e. vehicles registered outside London driving into London) however only ULEZ camera network is used in analysis. Method Discussion – NOx concentrations • Discussion of benefits of considering NOx concentrations and linking these with emissions. I.e. how have emissions changed and how has measured NOx changed? • Agreement this would be useful although public understanding of NOx less clear whilst focus for NO2 is important in relation heath impacts. • Discussed that providing NOx concentrations would support the methodology/process and provide internal sensitivity checks for method, although less useful for reporting. • Potential to use emissions impacts and infer attribution to concentration impacts. Method Discussion – Isolating the ULEZ impacts • Agreement that having control sites is a major benefit to the method. Isolating the ULEZ is good, but general agreement that presenting overall changes/trends in concentrations is more straightforward and simpler statistical analysis. • Noted that general trends already included but that these do not represent an impact and the report should continue to make this clear. • Discussion of the road increment calculation - the TfL methodology of using “outside background” rather than “inside London” background is a good idea. • Discuss about potential use of modelled concentration data similar to LAEI could be useful to use to help assess success? • Discussion that air pollution measurement data is more understandable and accepted when communicating with the public. LAEI inventory has regular update cycle with next one for baseline of 2022 due soon. • Counterfactual method discussed with reference to detailed method available in the ULEZ six month report. Method discussion – trend analysis • Discussed it could be useful to consider additional advanced method called seasonal trend decomposition using LOESS in order to help deal with seasonal cycles and sensitivity to LOESS span parameter. • Also discussed using moving average rather than LOESS which may be more understandable to general public. However sensitive to end dates of analysis and better for assessment undertaken when a longer time series is available. • Discussion that the starting point of impacts could be defined statistically with a change - detection - point algorithm. Consider the Buishand Range Test for change-point detection is available. • All recognised covid represents a major disrupter and make it difficult to identify a statistical starting point. Up until now, have used Mayoral announcement of scheme as starting point due to impact on pre- compliance/behaviour change. Method discussion – local assessments TFL asked the group for advice on how to conduct a more local impact analysis, e.g. borough-level, or if not feasible then could we use background to show the impacts for the wider population. • Agreed that analysis of impacts at specific hotspots would be valuable but it would be difficult to do a “No-ULEZ” scenario here. Maybe additional benefit of summarising the individual site changes in concentrations though not necessarily an impact. • Discussion of the London network of continuous monitoring sites. Other CAZs rely on diffusion tubes, which are much less accurate/granular. Option to use advanced method called “leave-out cross-validation”, which gives a level of strength of analysis. • For control sites- consider using the median to protect from sensitivity of outliers in data? • TfL asked if still appropriate to use aggregated “No ULEZ” scenario to compare with individual sites. It was agreed that given the number of sites it is still suitable but could underestimate the impacts of ULEZ and some sensitivity to local conditions represented in monitoring data. Method discussion – de-weathering approaches There a general discussion about the de-weathering approaches, and would this be suitable or a valuable addition to the ULEZ analysis? • It was agreed that the current method, i.e. looking at the sites around London as the control / counterfactual, is a more robust and suitable approach given the detailed datasets available. De-weathering approaches are useful in other settings but, for the key ULEZ analysis the current TfL method is better. Summary of how Paris LEZ was assessed • EF explained how the Paris LEZ was assessed. • LEZ began with Paris as first phase, then expanded to the Greater Paris metropolis. The impacts evaluation considers the Greater Paris metropolis with no distinction between phasing. • First step- estimates in pollutant trends. Based on the “Tale of Two Cities approach” (Font et al. 2019). Trends estimates were based on hourly concentrations for urban background and roadside to give estimates of how pollutant trends varied for different periods of the LEZ implementation. • To assess singular impact for LEZ, (Berlin evaluation method) looked at differences in fleet composition and did not use concentrations directly. Impact of Paris/Berlin LEZ was based on the difference in fleet composition and use calculated emissions calculated using simple model, then for each pollutant do the ratio of emissions between scenarios. Ratio (%) could potentially also be applied to pollutant trend. Contextualising AQ impacts to population exposure. • Discussed Belgian analysis - applies to annual average population information so it is difficult to do comparison. • Discussed potential to look at who lives along 30 m /roadside locations of major roads and apply a specific roadside location to an area. • TFL - we could look at population and possibly deprivation/BAME to describe number of people in these groups with benefits based on impacts at roadside using the method in the report. • Would be useful if we see if this can help demonstrate benefits in hotspots. • Belgium: study showing that people with lower socio-economic background live in more polluted areas. Transport Transport, or transportation, is moving people or things from one place to another place.[1] Transport can be divided into infrastructure, vehicles and operations. Infrastructure includes cableways, roads, railways, airports, canals and pipelines. The infrastructure is the network where things are carried. Infrastructure also includes airports, railway stations, bus stations and seaports (docks). Infrastructure is usually built by governments and paid for by taxes from the citizens of a country or region. Infrastructure such as roads and railways are designed by civil engineers and urban planners. Vehicles or vessels travel on the infrastructure. Vehicles include cable cars, cars, trucks, trains, spaceships and airplanes. Vehicles are usually designed by mechanical engineers. Vessels include boats, ferries, and barges which travel on canals and use docks and seaports. In the same way that trains use train stations, airplanes use airports. In the same way that trains use railway lines (train tracks), airplanes use flight paths and then fly in the sky.[2] Operations control the system. Operations include traffic signals, railway signals and air traffic control. Operations also include the government policies (a policy is a plan of action to guide decisions and actions) and regulations (a set or group of laws and rules) used to control the system, such as tolls, fuel taxes, and traffic laws. Transport and communications [change | change source] Transport and communication can be used instead of each other (someone could telephone a person rather than visit them). Transport traffic also needs communication. For example, air traffic control lets more airplanes fly. So, an increase of either transport or communication usually leads to an increase in the other one. Transport, energy, and the environment [change | change source] Transport uses a lot of energy. Trams, trolleybuses and trains use electricity and cycling is human-powered. Most transport uses hydrocarbons (oil and gas). This can create pollution. Environmental regulations (laws) and low-pollution fuels (for example liquified natural gas) can reduce pollution. But as more vehicles are used, more pollution is created. Ethanol and biodiesel pollute less than petroleum. Kinds of transportation [change | change source] Transport can be by cable, land, water or air: - Cable using cableways. e.g. cable cars and ski lifts etc. - Land transport using walking, roads and railway tracks.[3] by bicycles and other vehicles. e.g. buses, cars, trucks, trains, trams, bikes etc. - Water transport using ships and barges in canals, and in rivers and seas.[4] e.g. ships, submarines, jet skis etc. - Air transport using airplanes and airports and helicopters.[5] e.g. jets, aeroplanes etc. - Pipeline References [change | change source] - ↑ Transport in Japan, "What is transport?"; retrieved 2012-9-5. - ↑ Transport in Japan, "There are paths even in the air"; retrieved 2012-9-5. - ↑ Transport in Japan, "Land vehicles"; retrieved 2012-9-5. - ↑ Transport in Japan, "Sea vehicles"; retrieved 2012-9-5. - ↑ Transport in Japan, "Air vehicles"; retrieved 2012-9-5. 8 April 2019 the Mayor of London launched the world’s first 24-hour Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) in central London. On 25 October 2021 the zone was expanded across inner London, up to, but not including, the North and South Circular Roads. The ULEZ is now 18 times the size of the original area and covers four million people – around 44% of London’s population. The ULEZ does not operate in isolation. It operates in conjunction with the London- wide Low Emission Zone (LEZ), which was originally launched in 2008. It is the oldest of the capital’s emission control schemes and applies to large and heavy vehicles. In March 2021 enforcement of tougher emission standards for the LEZ began. Prior to this, the standards hadn’t changed since 2012. The LEZ standards are now the same as the ULEZ standards for most large and heavy vehicles. In this report we evaluate the impacts of the ULEZ and the LEZ schemes, focusing on one year following the ULEZ expansion to inner London and for the LEZ, over a year and a half on from the enforcement of tighter LEZ standards. The report, including the methodology for assessing impacts on air pollutant concentrations, underwent independent peer review1. The analyses addressed the impacts of the overall ULEZ scheme, differentiating the impacts by inner and central London zone where the data permitted this. Compliance rates are presented for the zone as a whole with further analysis looking at the central, ULEZ area, and the boundary roads. Fleet composition data is analysed for central, inner and outer London. Traffic impacts have been summarised for the ULEZ area, outside the ULEZ area and for the ULEZ boundary roads. Emissions impacts have been estimated for central, inner and outer London separately and as an average for London as a whole. Air pollution concentrations have been analysed per London zone with additional analysis looking at the impacts on the boundary roads. The findings indicate that the Mayor’s air quality policies, and in particular the ULEZ and LEZ schemes, are having a significant impact reducing the number of older, more polluting vehicles seen driving in London and on reducing the levels of harmful air pollution that Londoners are exposed to. In summary, the key findings are: Traffic and Vehicle Compliance • The vehicles traveling in London are increasingly cleaner. The overall ULEZ compliance rates have continued to increase, with 94.4 per cent of vehicles2 seen driving in the zone on an average day meeting the ULEZ standards a year following the expansion. This is an increase from just 39 per cent when the expansion was announced in 2017. • The number of older, more polluting vehicles in the zone has continued to reduce significantly. There was an almost 60 per cent reduction in non- 1 Peer reviewed by Dr Gary Fuller of Imperial College London 2 This excludes taxis and vehicles under the LEZ scheme. INNER LONDON ULTRA LOW EMISSION ZONE – ONE YEAR REPORT 6 compliant vehicles detected in the zone since the expansion came into operation, an average reduction of 74,000 polluting vehicles per day. • The heavy vehicle fleet is cleaner because of the London LEZ. The strengthening of emission standards resulted in a significant increase in compliance rates, such that compliance has now reached 97 per cent, increased from 90 per cent in February 2021, immediately prior to the tightening of the standards. • The proportion of diesel cars on London’s roads has reduced. In October 2022 the proportion of kilometres driven in London by diesel cars is estimated to have reduced from 32 per cent to about 25 per cent in inner London, showing the impact of the expansion in reducing diesel cars driving in inner London. In terms of private hire vehicles (PHVs), petrol hybrid electric vehicles comprise the largest proportion of this fleet. PHVs experienced an increase in the proportion of electric vehicles from October 2021 when the ULEZ was expanded, in both central and inner London. Changes to the composition of PHVs has been highly influenced by the additional licensing requirements for newly registered PHVs set by Transport for London to reduce emissions from these vehicles. • There has been an overall reduction in vehicles and traffic flows in the zone. In October 2022, there were 47,000 fewer vehicles3 seen in the zone on an average day (a reduction of almost 5 per cent) and data suggest traffic flows are around 3 per cent lower than in the weeks before the expansion. This is similar to the reduction in traffic flows observed following the introduction of the central London ULEZ. The COVID-19 pandemic also affected traffic levels. However, in outer London, traffic levels have largely returned to pre-pandemic levels but in central and inner London they remain below what they were in 2019. Air Pollutant Emissions4 • Pollution emissions have reduced dramatically. Cumulatively since 2019, it is estimated the ULEZ led to nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions from road traffic reducing by 13,500 tonnes across London over the four-year period compared with what they would have been without the ULEZ, a reduction of 23 per cent. Within the ULEZ area NOx emissions are estimated to have reduced by 5,000 tonnes, a reduction of 26 per cent, over the same period. Reductions in NOx emissions were seen across all vehicle types, but the greatest proportion was occurred in TfL busses at 70%. Cumulatively, emissions of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) are estimated to have reduced by 180 tonnes across London since 2019, compared to without the ULEZ, a reduction of 7 per cent. Within the ULEZ area PM2.5 emissions are estimated to have reduced by 80 tonnes, a reduction of 19 per cent, over the same period. 3 This excludes taxis and vehicles under the LEZ scheme 4 Emissions are the amount of pollution directly emitted from a particular source, e.g vehicles. INNER LONDON ULTRA LOW EMISSION ZONE – ONE YEAR REPORT 7 • Carbon emissions from vehicles have also reduced. Cumulatively since 2019 it is estimated the ULEZ has led to a reduction of around 800,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions from vehicles across London over the four-year period compared to without the ULEZ, a saving of 3 per cent. Within the ULEZ area this is a saving of 290,000 tonnes, a reduction of 4 per cent over the same period. Air Pollutant Concentrations5 • The air in the zone is substantially cleaner. The ULEZ expansion has led to four million people breathing cleaner air, including 1,362 more schools. Harmful nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentrations are estimated to be 21 per cent lower than they would have been in inner London without the ULEZ and 46 per cent lower than they would have been in central London. This is above what was predicted for the scheme. Substantial reductions in NO2 concentrations were seen at roadside locations, with a 56 per cent reduction in central London, 47 per cent in inner London, and 37 per cent in outer London since 2017. Background monitoring sites away from the main road network also had significant reductions in NO2 of 47 per cent in central and 45 per cent in inner London, since 2017. Unlike central and inner London sites, average concentrations at outer London background sites have remained constant since 2021. • The boundary roads have also benefited from cleaner air. All air quality monitoring sites on the boundary roads recorded large reductions in NO2 concentrations and there has been an estimated reduction of 19 - 27 per cent compared to a scenario without the ULEZ with the impact increasing over time. Showing therefore there has been no displacement of pollution to the boundary. • NO2 levels have not returned to those experienced pre-pandemic, indicating that even as traffic levels have risen; cleaner vehicles in the fleet caused by the ULEZ and its expansion, have had sustained and positive impacts on air pollution meaning concentrations continue to be far below what they would have been otherwise. • Particulate matter (PM2.5) levels have also continued to reduce across London with a 41 per cent reduction in average concentrations in central and inner London since 2017. The findings set out in this report show that both the ULEZ and the LEZ continue to have a significant impact on the number of older, more polluting vehicles seen driving in London and on reducing harmful air pollution. In September 2021, shortly before the expansion of the ULEZ to inner London, the World Health Organization (WHO) strengthened its ambient air quality guidelines (AQGs) in recognition of the growing body of health evidence that continued to show 5 Concentration is the amount of pollution in the air at a certain location. The latest WHO AQGs are more stringent than UK legal limits for air quality and show that further action will be needed to tackle emissions from both transport and non-transport sources of air pollution in order to meet the guidelines and protect health. This includes taking action in outer London given that average concentrations at background monitoring sites in outer London have remained constant since 2021. Further expansion of the ULEZ to outer London will help improve air quality for millions more Londoners. INNER LONDON ULTRA LOW EMISSION ZONE – ONE YEAR REPORT 9 Introduction Toxic air pollution is a matter of life and death and affects Londoners in all stages of life. Studies have long shown the many adverse health issues associated with elevated pollution levels, with toxic air contributing to the premature deaths of an estimated 4,000 Londoners in 20196 and to over 1,700 hospitalisations related to asthma and COPD7 in 2017-2019, and to increasing the risk of dementia8 and lung cancer9. Over 600,000 Londoners live with a lung condition and are more vulnerable to the impacts of air pollution, with more than half of these people living in outer London. We also know that exposure to toxic air is disproportionally higher for those communities that have higher levels of deprivation, or a higher proportion of people from Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic backgrounds10, though, due to air quality policies implemented since 2016, the gap is now narrowing. Aimed at reducing the health impacts associated with high pollution levels in London, the Mayor of London introduced the world’s first 24 hour Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ) in central London on the 8 April 2019. The central London ULEZ delivered substantial impacts on air pollution, with nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentrations in central London reducing by 37 per cent, compared to a scenario without the ULEZ, in the first 10 months. In order to increase the number of Londoners benefiting from the impacts of the ULEZ, on the 25 October 2021, the Mayor expanded the ULEZ to 18 times its original size, covering the area within the North and South Circular Roads and the four million people that reside within. Six months following the expansion of the ULEZ, NO2 concentrations had reduced by 44 per cent in central London and 20 per cent in inner London, compared with a scenario without the ULEZ. The London Low Emission Zone (LEZ) was first introduced in 2008, applying to heavy vehicles. In the most recent change to the LEZ, the emission limits were tightened on 1 March 2021 and now align with the ULEZ standards for most affected vehicles. Tackling air pollution is a matter of social justice and hence a key priority for the Mayor. The ULEZ is one of many bold policies implemented to address this and is recognised by independent experts as one of the most effective and speedy interventions. This report evaluates the impacts of the October 2021 expansion of the ULEZ scheme in its first full year of operation, up to the end of October 2022. What is the ULEZ? The expansion of the ULEZ to Inner London is the latest in a progression of policies aimed at tackling harmful air pollution emissions from road transport, specifically nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, by disincentivising the use of older, more polluting vehicles within the Ultra Low Emission Zone through applying a daily charge to vehicles that do not meet the emissions criteria. Emissions criteria are based on the Euro standards which regulate the emissions of pollutants from road vehicles as they are sold. The Euro standards emission limits have progressively reduced over time, meaning vehicles have become less polluting with each successive standard. Figure 1: Timeline of successive emission-based charging schemes in London Figure 1 above shows the timeline of emissions-based charge schemes in London including consultations, the T-charge which preceded the ULEZ, and the tightening of the LEZ standards. The ULEZ operates 24 hours a day, every day of the year except Christmas Day (25 December). Vehicles must meet strict emission standards to drive in the ULEZ area: • Euro 4 for petrol cars and small vans (registered new from January 2006) • Euro 6 for diesel cars and small vans (registered new from September 2015) • Euro 3 for motorcycles and other L-category vehicles (registered new from July 2007) INNER LONDON ULTRA LOW EMISSION ZONE – ONE YEAR REPORT 11 Vehicles that do not meet these standards must pay a charge of £12.50 per day to travel in the zone. Figure 2 shows the area of London covered by the initial central ULEZ and the ULEZ expansion up to the North and South Circular roads. Figure 2: Map of the central London ULEZ and the current ULEZ boundary What is the London-wide Low Emission Zone (LEZ)? The London-wide Low Emission Zone was introduced in 2008 and operates 24 hours a day, every day of the year. On 1 March 2021 the emission standards for the LEZ were strengthened for heavy vehicles, the new standards are: • Euro VI for buses, coaches and Heavy Goods Vehicles (HGVs)/vans over 3.5 tonnes (vehicles registered new from September 2016), • Euro 3 for particulate matter only for vans between 1.2 tonnes and 3.5 tonnes and minibuses under 5t (vehicles registered new from January 2001). Vehicles that do not meet these standards must pay a charge of £100 per day. Heavy vehicles that do not meet the lower Euro IV standard must pay a higher charge of £300 per day. INNER LONDON ULTRA LOW EMISSION ZONE – ONE YEAR REPORT 12 For most vehicles, the strengthening of the LEZ standards means that they are not separately subject to LEZ and ULEZ standards. The exception is for vans between 1.2t and 3.5t, and minibuses under 5t where the LEZ and ULEZ standards are different. These vehicles need to comply with both schemes if they drive within the ULEZ area or pay both sets of charges. The expansion will come into effect on Tuesday 29 August 2023 and will operate across all London boroughs up to the existing Low Emission Zone boundary. This report will look at the first full year of monitoring data and will provide the first analysis of the impact of the expanded ULEZ on air pollution emissions. As such, the impacts of the ULEZ are rigorously monitored and the success of the ULEZ can be assessed through a number of different metrics: • Number of vehicles and compliance rates • Changes in fleet composition • Traffic flow data • Modelling of vehicle NOx and PM emissions • Modelling of vehicle carbon emissions • Air quality monitoring Number of vehicles and compliance rates Vehicle compliance rate refers to the proportion of vehicles that meet the ULEZ/LEZ emission standards. Fleet compositions The fleet composition is the mix of vehicles, split by vehicle type and fuel type, that travel in London and is a key input for estimating the emissions from vehicles and the changes in emissions due to the ULEZ and associated policies. As London’s vehicle fleet becomes cleaner as a result of the Mayor’s policies, emissions from vehicles operating in London are expected to reduce. Both the ULEZ and LEZ influence the fleet composition because they incentivise the uptake of cleaner vehicles above and beyond the natural turnover of vehicles that would be expected. Fleet composition (including fuel types) are based on a proportion of the total vehicle kilometres driven rather than vehicle numbers, as some vehicles travel much further than others (e.g. delivery drivers, private hire vehicles). For the purposes of this report, we refer to the fleet composition representing the proportion of kilometres estimated by vehicle type and fuel type (and power train). The data used in this section has been based on data analysis of observations using TfL’s camera network. Monthly information on changes to the fleet composition have been compiled for this report including information from February 2019, just prior to the launch of the ULEZ in central London in April 2019. The monthly fleet composition information can be used to estimate the changes in emissions from vehicles over time as the proportions of mileage, especially by compliant vehicles, increases, and changes in fuel types are taken into account. Monthly fluctuations are visible in the dataset because they are representing different levels of activity including during Covid lockdowns, holiday periods, as well as reflecting immediate scheme impacts during and after implementation. Fleet composition changes would also include the impacts of the Mayor’s scrappage schemes14 that have been particularly successful in encouraging modal shift away from vehicles, with a third of recipients not replacing their vehicles. The ULEZ aims to tackle the triple threats of air pollution, the climate emergency and congestion. By introducing minimum emission standards for vehicles the ULEZ is likely to deter a small proportion of trips or lead to a change in how people travel. Traffic flows are also an important input for estimating the impacts of the ULEZ on pollution emissions, which are provided in the next section of the report. Many factors influence traffic patterns in London. Traffic normally follows a usual pattern of seasonal variation with lower levels in holiday periods. However, in recent years there have been a number of additional factors which have had significant impacts on traffic levels. The lockdowns and changes to working patterns due to the Covid-19 pandemic led to greatly reduced traffic flows in 2020 and also in 2021, particularly in central London. TfL’s Travel in London Report16 provides further detailed analysis on the impacts of the pandemic on transport. The fuel shortages and following price crisis may have and continue to influence traffic, however the recent Travel in London Report has yet to find evidence of this. Therefore, it has not been possible to identify fully the sole and direct impact of the ULEZ on traffic flows. Data Sources The data described in this section is based on automatic traffic count (ATC) data from Department for Transport (DfT), Highways England and TfL’s ATC Network. As with the fleet composition, the data is presented as vehicle kilometres rather than numbers of unique vehicles detected, as used in the previous section on numbers of vehicles and compliance rates. Using vehicle kilometres as an indicator of traffic levels gives a better indication of the traffic flows than using the number of unique vehicles detected, as certain vehicles will be on the roads for longer and may travel through the zone multiple times a day. The DfT data for 2022 is yet to be released so figures for 2022 are solely based upon TfL’s ATC network.
